changes.change: post() and ack() commit each part's attempt with the bridge's outbox authority (delivery_store) before any of its bytes, record each part's outcome (confirmed, refused, rejected, or ended without or with finality after an absolute wait and a bounded drain), and on a failure hand off the unconfirmed remainder or queue the whole call (a connection a failed record closed is never used again); with no committed answer they publish one immutable fallback file per call instead, and raise Queued only once it is durable. Login and channel creation have absolute deadlines, and a part's confirmation deadline also bounds each buffered line and each PONG written for a buffered PING; an active deadline bounds every write, login and channel setup included. A silent run's post is refused and never queued in any form. outbox_append(), outbox_claim(), outbox_summary(), reserve() and queued_entry() are removed: this release writes no outbox.jsonl row.

changes.change: post(), ack() and deliver_entry() are each one section of writer admission: admission.lock held shared (taken without blocking, a miss read as held maintenance) from before the first create, queue or fallback publication to the end of the call, with the maintenance record read while holding it. A held or unreadable record, or a `maintenance` reply to any request, keeps the call whole as one immutable file in the refusal sink refused.d/ (with any attestation of an outcome or void the authority did not record) and raises Held, a kind of Queued; a lock that cannot be created fails as an unwritable outbox does; the bridge's own entry delivery starts nothing under maintenance.

changes.change: The bridge runs the outbox authority (delivery_store.Authority: the only opener of outbox.db, on its own thread, serving outbox.sock; started all or nothing, and started again whole at the next pass after any failure or a dead thread) and its flush, in which one step's or one item's failure never stops another: it imports fallback files and the legacy outbox without outbox.lock, ends gone writers' attempts, abandons (E8) or, for its own announcements, adopts (E9) their entries, reconciles from current state (R1, R2), dead-letters after 24 hours with a content-free alert row, gives every eligible entry its attempt, and retires claims and writes dead letters under a bounded outbox.lock. It indexes every verified message (V1) before its checkpoint moves, with the server's own time, msgid and account only (one without them is a failed index, never given a local substitute); a new channel gets a durable replay boundary when joined, from the server's join time only (without one: no coverage from that join, and a boundary before all of its history); a failed index invalidates any catch-up of that channel, which completes nothing until a replay from the preserved checkpoint indexes it; keeps record coverage in the authority, writes the pending queue, ledger and dead letters durably (a delivery leaves only once its ledger line is durable, and one that cannot be written blocks no other), and announces with a derived entry id, saving held_announced only once the announcement is durable; an interrupt records its durable intent before its first agent-affecting command, and takes none without it; one that may have acted without a proved submission, or is found in intent after a restart, is held, never rung again, settled only by exact-identity proof in the ledger or by its acknowledgement, and otherwise dead-lettered truthfully; a delivered interrupt's ledger line, announcement and the save of its state are each done again until durable, across its acknowledgement or dead letter; an acknowledgement already recorded settles each recipient's interrupt after a restart, read again until it succeeds, including after a live settling fails in the ledger; a replayed message adds no second interrupt for the same recipient, an interrupt counts as queued only once saved, and a new one reopens acknowledgement recovery; an acknowledgement counts as recorded only once durable (delivery_store.durable_append), and while acks.jsonl cannot be read the interrupts it could settle are neither rung nor dead-lettered; for the pending, acknowledgement and ledger files only a missing file is absence, and any other failure to inspect or read one is unknown, never empty; a line read from acks.jsonl, or a ledger line taken as an interrupt's proof, counts only once the file and its directory are synced; an interrupt's intent is committed only once the state directory's ancestry is durable, and acknowledgement recovery reopens when recovery accepts or holds an interrupt; only a missing pending.json is an empty queue, and one that cannot be read or parsed is never replaced, nothing new is queued and nothing delivered until it can be read; and each owner alert's dead letter is its own (#19 owner amendment 6, 2026-10-10). The file-based claimed-outbox, reservation and attribution state is removed.

changes.change: The bridge holds while a maintenance record exists or cannot be read: each message, join, catch-up completion, acknowledgement, coverage update at a PONG, delivery pass, flush lock, flush step and entry delivery is one section of writer admission, and a section that finds the record held starts nothing, closes the connection and puts the bridge in a hold that reads the record every HOLD_RECHECK seconds. It starts no authority, writes no status snapshot (the unavailable one included), and logs the holder once per change. After the release it catches up from its checkpoints and imports the refusal sink with outbox.d/. An authority whose close was deferred by maintenance is kept, not dropped with its database open, and closed at a later pass.

changes.change: The bridge applies the activation's designation bootstrap (designation-bootstrap/1) at its authority's start. Its one launch option, --activation-bootstrap sha256:<D>, names the record; before any database open it checks the record's exact bytes against D, the schema, its own running release and the actual state root, and inside the authority's opening transaction it classifies the committed bootstrap row: no activation (S1); a first commit that designates the listed accounts (none for an explicit empty list) and records the operation, digest, effective time and version (S2); or an exact replay that changes nothing and never designates again (S3). Any other state is UNKNOWN: the authority does not start, nothing is committed (not even the epoch), deleted or rewritten, the status snapshot is not replaced, and the bridge neither serves nor recovers until it is resolved. Every field of the record and of the committed row is checked for its exact type before anything compares or sorts it, the record is read through one descriptor of the state root, and anything that can't be judged is UNKNOWN, never an ordinary failure (code review slot 2 on PR #22). The validated state root's descriptor is held through the authority's whole start: the state path must still name it before anything opens, inside the opening transaction before any commit, after the commit and around the bind, or the state is UNKNOWN (code review slot 3 on PR #22). The validated realpath is revalidated with that identity, so a root moved behind a symlink is UNKNOWN, and for an activated launch a database whose bootstrap state can't be read, classified or committed is UNKNOWN, never an ordinary failure (code review 6112483129 on PR #22), as is startup metadata of the wrong shape; and the root and the database are checked once more inside the opening transaction after the bootstrap's designations and M, immediately before COMMIT, so drift rolls them back (PR #22 review 1); the database is bound to the very file SQLite opened (one this process holds open), so a database put at its name since is UNKNOWN (PR #22 review 2); and for a launch with no activation, M is classified at the first metadata read, and a failure before M is shown absent on a database that already existed is UNKNOWN (PR #22 review 3); for every launch while S1 is unproven (an activated one, or one with no digest), an existing outbox.db is classified read-only through the pinned root before the authority opens it (not SQLite in WAL mode, or with a rollback journal: UNKNOWN, every byte kept), and a failed start removes only its own socket, through the pinned root and by its identity (PR #22 review 4); its directory-relative effects go through the pinned root, and the root is checked immediately before and after the pathname-based database open and socket bind (#21 amendment 7); an activated start pins the root before its outer section, so even that section's admission lock is opened through it, and an existing WAL database is classified on a private copy (outbox.db and its -wal, read through the pinned root) before any writable open, so no checkpoint or sidecar change can happen to the evidence (PR #22 review R1); a database is new only when no outbox.db, -wal, -shm or -journal exists, or an empty outbox.db has no sidecar, any other evidence being UNKNOWN, and the copy must match this authority's schema exactly and run the very opening transaction, bootstrap application included, before the original is opened for writing (PR #22 review 2/4). Under writer admission the whole start is one section: it holds while any maintenance record exists, except that a full record binding this launch's operation, digest and release admits the start, which then serves read-only status only (#21 amendment 4, K3).

The isolation guard fails closed on real state, the network and live agents.
Every pchat subcommand and option SKILL.md mentions exists in the captured pchat (PLT-15); the held-call guidance describes exit 5 (#24).
Message-ID deduplication after acceptance recovery, across a crash, a restart and a restart after a cut-short catch-up of six full pages (PLT-15 requirement 8).

The outbox's one SQLite authority (#19): the store and its transitions, reconciliation, the bridge-only authority server and its request protocol, clients, fallback files and the lock-free import (design revision 8); and writer admission (#24, docs/writer_admission.md): the maintenance record reader, the admission-lock sections, per-transaction admission and the `maintenance` reply, the refusal sink and its import, the authority's start and its failure cleanup as one section, a close that waits for a section or the release, and the owning operation's fenced primitives (Owner), whose recovery adopts only the file it published and makes what it recovers durable before it journals it; and the bound start (#21 amendment 4, K3): a `full` record whose binding is the launch's operation, digest and release admits the bridge's start as one operation-owned section, held from the admission through classification, the start, the socket's binding and a failed start's cleanup; and the pinned root of that activated start (#21 amendment 7): every effect the standard library can make directory-relative (the authority lock, the admission lock of its start section, outbox.d, a stale socket's removal, a failed start's own socket) goes through the validated root's descriptor, while the database's open and the socket's bind stay pathname-based; and Owner's optional root_fd, through which the owning operation's admission lock is made and opened (PR #22 review 2/4).
Shared fakes for the outbox tests: a chat server that commits before it answers, an injected clock, invented processes, an in-process authority and a filesystem model that drops unsynced changes.
#19's failing-first regressions: the whole-post repost, a failed confirmation record and a stopped outbox.lock holder, run against the code before and after the fix.
#19's acceptance 1-10 and design revision 8's posting scenarios against a fake server and an in-process authority.
The outbox authority's rules: attribution, finality, fragments, accounting on every part, collection, alerts, A12 and attested outcomes (#19).
The outbox's file boundaries: fallback files, the legacy claim and durable exports, with power losses and a stopped lock holder (#19).

The bridge-only authority and its request protocol over socketpairs: stopped clients, floods, replays, epochs, unavailability and the one opener (#19). Its no-designation-interface test admits only the bridge's one bootstrap commit (#21).

The bridge's outbox side: coverage and indexing, bounded setup, its announcements and E9, and the authority thread (#19). The designation bootstrap at the authority's start: S1, S2, S3 and every UNKNOWN state, crashes and retries (#21). Malformed but digest-matching records and malformed committed rows are UNKNOWN (PR #22). A state root swapped after classification, or moved behind a symlink, is UNKNOWN; so is a database whose bootstrap state can't be read, or whose startup metadata has the wrong shape, through ensure_authority() and main(); a root moved during the bootstrap's application rolls it back, a database replaced before its identity is captured is UNKNOWN, and so is a committed M with no launch digest and unreadable startup metadata; a non-WAL database is UNKNOWN with every byte kept, a failed start keeps a foreign socket, a root swapped around the start or the bind fails closed with the lock and outbox.d only in the pinned root, an outstanding WAL is kept byte-identical when classification is UNKNOWN, a swap before the first admission lock leaves none in the replacement, orphaned or empty-database sidecars are UNKNOWN and kept, and a database missing a required table is UNKNOWN and kept (PR #22).
A crash at every boundary of design revision 8's section 5.5, one case per row (#19).

Shared fakes for the writer-admission tests (#24): an invented journal for the owning operation, byte snapshots of a state directory, a guard against any blocking flock, and a base case that holds invented maintenance on the sandboxed state.

The maintenance record's reader and the admission-lock sections: no file admitted, a valid record held, anything else unknown and held, and a reader that never writes (#24; writer admission 4.2, 4.3).

The owning operation's primitives under a caller-supplied journal or fence: acquire, drain, advance, release and a read-only reconcile, with crash, resume, pending-effect, evidence and fence-failure cases (#24; design tests 3, 5-8, reduced).

Clients under maintenance: a refusal keeps exactly one sink file and changes nothing else in the boundary; exit 5 and the notice line; delayed marker for posts and notices and none for acknowledgements; the admission table on every execution path; read-only status and query (#24; design tests 2, 5, 13; A3, A5).

Draining, a paused client and lock ordering with real threads: a call in progress finishes while new ones are refused, the authority's selector thread never sleeps, and no acquisition blocks (#24; design tests 1 and 10, A2, the ordering and deadlock schedule).

The bridge under maintenance: the hold, the authority start refused under any record, no database, WAL or socket created, flush steps and the status snapshot held, and resumption after the release (#24; design test 9, reduced).

The bridge's bound start under a full record (#21 amendment 4, K3; design test 9): held in partial and under any record not this launch's; under its own full record the bootstrap commits once, status answers with the record and the epoch, every mutation gets maintenance and nothing else runs; L_adm held shared through classification, start, bind and cleanup; socket and thread failures released and retried; a close outside any section deferred until the release.

The two import sources: the refusal sink beside outbox.d/ with source identity, entry-id deduplication, basename collisions, bounded fairness, listing failures and the import pass's accounting (#24; A4).

The request/v1 one-line request form: strict parsing and canonical encoding, the logical-content digest and request-scoped authority validation against injected evidence. A pure library that nothing calls yet (COLLAB-1, #27).

request/v1 round trip, refusal of non-canonical forms, digest stability, conflicting reuse and the verified, unresolved and refused outcomes, in eight offline scenarios on invented data (COLLAB-1, #27).

Owner accounts (#29, staged slice 1): the exact, server-verified owner account rule and its refusals, a malformed or absent optional list, the second account's routing and waiting-owner authority, and one owner push per post with none from an owner account, in three offline scenarios on invented data.
An invented example of the private owner-led file (#31, amendment 3): the legacy scope and the protected workspace and surface ids. Documentation only: no code reads it.

Owner-led routing in plateia (#31): the private file's every valid and invalid form, fail-closed routing and its fixed-token evidence with the review-start experiment on and off, #29's owner identity rule (second account, malformed list, unverified nick, replay), protected workspaces and surfaces, hook failure, and writer admission (a held owner post, acknowledge() inside its own section), on invented data.

working_copy.note: The owner's exception to D-19 for #31 only (amendments 1 to 3, 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-15): five files are captured from the skills repository's working copy, uncommitted bytes over this HEAD, because owner-led routing was never committed there. Each such entry's `working_copy` records the source bytes' sha256, apart from the sanitized repository file's `sha256`, which intentionally differs and lists how in `changes`. chat-bridge's source is the pre-change bytes holding only the owner-led hookup, so the live chat-bridge, which also holds other uncaptured changes, stays reported as changed. No baseline content is invented for the three files the baseline never had (their `baseline` is null). A live file at its recorded working-copy bytes is reported as `working copy`, never as a carried commit.
